messages.subject: candidating a project
parts:
Hi all I set up a project, markovchain, on which I am the main mentor. I am receiving many email of interest from students. I do not know which is the process of my project approval, selection and the student evaluation: 

a. Regarding the students... How do they submit a project (they are said so submit to google melange). I should rate it but to whom I have to communicate my selection?
b. Regarding the projects... When funded project will be selected?

Thanks

messages.author: b98e21751c27e8b9
messages.subject: Re: candidating a project
parts:
On Fri, 2015-03-20 at 13:56 -0700, Giorgio Spedicato wrote:
> Hi all I set up a project, markovchain, on which I am the main mentor.
> I am receiving many email of interest from students. I do not know
> which is the process of my project approval, selection and the student
> evaluation:
>

All mentors must request to be part of the R project on melange. please
include a link in your request note to your project idea and to your
credentials if you are not already known to the R GSoC program
administrators.

>
> a. Regarding the students... How do they submit a project (they are
> said so submit to google melange). I should rate it but to whom I have
> to communicate my selection?

Students must submit project applications on melange.

The student application process is open till the end of next week.
Incomplete applications will be disallowed by the R GSoC Administrators.

As in past years, all R student applications will be rated by all R
mentors.

While the applications are being commented on and rated by the R
mentors, the R GSoC Administrators will request slots from Google based
on the number of mentors and high quality applications for projects
received.

Google will grant us a certain number of slots. that number has ranged
from half of our requested slots to two slots more than we asked for in
prior years.

> b. Regarding the projects... When funded project will be selected?
>

As has been the case in prior years, once Google grants us slots, we
will award them to the top rated projects and applications.

It is important to note that per longstanding R GSoC process, we will
also disallow any project that does not have two mentors, a project with
both mentors who have never participated in GSoC, mentors who we cannot
verify, and in most but not all cases projects where both mentors are
from the same institution (especially if you have no prior GSoC
experience).

It is also important that per Google program guidelines (you clicked on
them in melange), communication with students during the application
period be limited to feedback on their applications. Only Google can
notify students that they have been accepted to the program.

Regards,

Brian

--

Hi Brian,

I would volunteer to help co-mentor any Markov chain or Viterbi beam
search project, if I am invited.

I note since http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rgp/index.html
is including symbolic regressions, I would be glad to mentor a project
to add adjustments for model degrees of freedom to its goodness of fit
scores.

I am also happy to provide comments on proposals. If someone wants to
build a system to trade ahead of index fund rebalancing, I will be
extremely unlikely to support it.

Best regards,
James Salsman

messages.author: b98e21751c27e8b9
messages.subject: Re: candidating a project

On 03/22/2015 04:17 AM, Bernd Bischl wrote:
> Dear Brian Peterson,
>
> > a project with both mentors who have never participated in GSoC,
>
> is that an absolute statement? I have not seen this info before
> unfortunately. Was that visible somewhere? I guess that would rule out
> all 3 mlr projects that we have put up, as all of us would be first time
> gsoc mentors. Michel has taken part as a student in GSOC before.
>
> We have now invested considerable work for project creation,
> organization and student communication and testing and that would really
> be an unfortunate turn of events.

This has been a long-standing guideline of R's participation in GSoC.

Some of this information was on the old sciviews R wiki, which was
unfortunately taken down rather suddenly.

All of the things I mentioned are guidelines built from many years of
R's participation in GSoC. All of them have been broken at one point or
another, and usually hinge on comfort with the student proposals and
mentor preparation. (To this last point, is is promising that you
mention that you have been preparing for a long time for your mlr projects.)

Another guideline which you are running up against is that you propose
three projects for your first GSoC. As Michel should be able to tell
you, GSoC is a *lot* of work for the mentors as well as the students. I
personally will be very unlikely to support not one but *three* projects
from a group of participants among whom only one has any GSoC experience.

First, you would have to have three really excellent proposals, such
that they filtered to the upper grouping of the voting.

Next, you, as mentors, would have to make clear how you are going to
make time to mentor that many students. It has been done. I was primary
mentor on one project, and listed as co-mentor on three others a few
years ago. Of those, I had significant involvement in two of the
projects I was co-mentoring. In this my experience is much like the
model you're proposing.

That summer, I spent 30+ hours per week mentoring those GSoC projects.
I have not tried to do that in subsequent years, because it is just too
much of a commitment in addition to my full time work at the office. Do
you and your co-mentors *each* have that much time?

Finally, R would have to receive enough slots from Google for all of
your projects to get slots. I'm sure you can understand that slots are
a finite commodity, and giving three slots to one group and zero slots
to other projects if applications are comparable would not be fair.

So, is this a hard and fast rule? No, not at all. Will it be an issue
for you? That depends first on the quality of your applications. Only
if you get excellent student proposals for all three of your proposed
projects and R asks for and receives lots of slots will we be having a
conversation about whether you and your co-mentors really have the time
to dedicate to this.

Regards,

Brian

--
Brian G. Peterson

Regarding our number of projects:

We have put the same amount of work into each of the proposals, and
tried to achieve good ones,
but as the mlr project has grown rather large and students have
different interests and backgrounds, we wanted to use that chance to get
the best thing(s) done in the end. Even without your email we were aware
that there is a high possibility that not all 3 proposals might be
selected in the end. But we thought our process improves the possibility
that the right people together to something very worthhile.

Regarding mentors / time:

I am mainly mentoring the hyperparameter / tuning project, that I am
doing research on anyway.
And I am willing to put that much time in.

The visualization project is mentored by 2 other very competent people.
As our software is like I said not small, I am mainly "guiding" here,
if someone gets stuck on a complex design question.

For the ensemble one, Aydin is the main mentor nad has also done lots of
work with apllying students.

We also already communicated a lot with promising students. Some already
did very nice pull request, which are beyond simple tests and already
helping the project "for free". We did that to minimize technical /
organizational friction in the beginning.

If only one project would be selected, it is also very likely that some
of the other mentors switwch over to help (cannot force anybody, but I
would do that, if, e.g our visualization project is only selected).
So the burden would be further shared.

Thanks for your detailed feedback, it helped us "GSOC newcomers". I
really like the general spirit of this thing and hope we can make
something work.

Best

Bernd
